title: Complex numbers
lede: What happens when you take the square root of a negative number. Imaginary sounds made-up, but engineers use these numbers every day to design power grids, phones and audio.

sections.md:
## The imaginary unit
No real number squared gives a negative. So mathematicians defined one:

**i = √−1, so i² = −1**

Then √−25 = √25 · √−1 = **5i**.

A **complex number** has a real part and an imaginary part: **a + bi**.
- 3 + 4i: real part 3, imaginary part 4.
- 7 is complex too (7 + 0i). Every real number is a complex number with b = 0.

The name *imaginary* was originally meant as an insult (it's often credited to Descartes). It stuck, but these numbers are as legitimate as negatives, which were also once considered absurd.

## Powers of i cycle
| Power | Value |
|---|---|
| i¹ | i |
| i² | −1 |
| i³ | −i |
| i⁴ | 1 |
| i⁵ | i (starts over) |

The cycle repeats every 4. To find iⁿ, divide n by 4 and use the **remainder**: i³⁰ → 30 ÷ 4 leaves 2 → i³⁰ = i² = **−1**.

## Arithmetic
**Add/subtract:** combine real parts and imaginary parts separately.
(3 + 2i) + (5 − 7i) = **8 − 5i**

**Multiply:** distribute like binomials, then replace i² with −1.
(2 + 3i)(4 − i) = 8 − 2i + 12i − 3i² = 8 + 10i + 3 = **11 + 10i**

**Conjugates:** the conjugate of a + bi is **a − bi**. Their product is always real:
(a + bi)(a − bi) = a² + b²
(3 + 4i)(3 − 4i) = 9 + 16 = **25**

**Divide:** multiply top and bottom by the conjugate of the bottom, to clear i from the denominator.

sections.title: Division
steps: Multiply by the conjugate (1 − 2i) on top and bottom.

sections.md:
## Where they show up first: quadratics
When the discriminant b² − 4ac is **negative**, the quadratic formula gives complex roots, always as a **conjugate pair**.

**x² + 2x + 5 = 0**: discriminant 4 − 20 = −16. x = (−2 ± √−16) ÷ 2 = (−2 ± 4i) ÷ 2 = **−1 ± 2i**.

With complex numbers, every degree-n polynomial has **exactly n roots** (counting multiplicity). That's the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra from earlier.

## The complex plane
Plot a + bi as the point **(a, b)**: real part on the horizontal axis, imaginary part on the vertical. Now complex numbers are **points**, or arrows from the origin.

- The **modulus** (size) is the distance from the origin: **|a + bi| = √(a² + b²)**. |3 + 4i| = 5.
- Multiplying by **i** rotates a point **90° counterclockwise**: 1 → i → −1 → −i → 1. That's why powers of i cycle every 4: four quarter-turns make a full turn.

That rotation property is why electrical engineers use complex numbers to describe alternating current, where voltage and current go around in cycles. Phones, audio and image compression rely on the same math.

sections.label: Common traps
sections.md:
- **i² = −1, not 1.** Replace it every time.
- **√(−4) · √(−9) ≠ √36.** Convert to i first: 2i · 3i = 6i² = −6.
- **Complex roots come in conjugate pairs** for polynomials with real coefficients.
- **Real numbers are complex numbers** with imaginary part 0.

practice.why: Flip the sign of the imaginary part.
Multiply by (2 − i): top (10 − 5i)(2 − i) = 20 − 10i − 10i + 5i² = 15 − 20i. Bottom 4 + 1 = 5. Result: **3 − 4i**.
practice.hint: Multiply top and bottom by the conjugate.

practice.q: Multiplying 2 + 0i by i twice moves it to…
practice.why: Each multiplication by i rotates 90° counterclockwise: 2 → 2i → −2. Two quarter-turns = a half-turn.
